idiom_name: keyed in-flight registry + shareable completion handle + forget-on-completion
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: derive the key from every result-affecting input, then atomically register an entry for that key in a concurrent registry. The caller that wins the registration becomes the leader and performs the computation exactly once; every other caller finds the entry, joins the flight and observes the shared completion handle for the value or error. The leader publishes the outcome to all current and late waiters and removes the key from the registry, so the structure holds only genuinely in-flight work - result retention is a separate decision with a separate owner (memoization/cache-aside). Give waiters a way to leave as well as a way to join (abandon the wait on timeout or cancellation while the flight continues for the others), keep the registry lock off the computation path, and bound both the key cardinality and the flight duration.
code_sketch:
key = derive(op, params, tenant, authz_scope)      # all result-affecting inputs
entry = registry.compute_if_absent(key):            # atomic: one leader per key
    leader(key)                                     # this caller runs the work
# waiters: entry.wait() -> shared value | shared error
# leader: entry.publish(value|error); registry.forget(key)
pitfalls: Keeping the entry after the flight completes silently converts the coalescer into an unbounded, never-invalidated result cache.
A key that omits tenant or authorisation scope coalesces different principals; the shared result is then a data leak, not a speed-up.
Letting the first waiter's timeout or cancellation cancel the shared computation breaks every other waiter.

Trusting a leader/shared flag for metrics or logic: the shared indicator is timing-sensitive (golang/go#74880 disputed exactly this under contention), so instrument flights and waiters explicitly instead of inferring them from the return value.

No escape hatch for the wait: production collapsers give waiters a bounded wait and then let some of them through (nginx proxy_cache_lock_timeout releases waiters to the origin; proxy_cache_lock_age re-admits if the in-flight request stalls) - a coalescer where every waiter waits forever converts a stampede into a pile-up behind one stuck flight.

One global lock around the key map: the classic single Group serializes registrations for all keys, so at high throughput the coalescer becomes the bottleneck it was meant to remove - shard the registry when the mutex shows up in profiles.
